case_study_insert.main_stem: Velvette Beauty (VB) is a private limited company in the beauty and cosmetics retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2019 by Amara Osei, the pure-player brand sells skincare and cosmetics online from its Norwood fulfilment centre under a flat structure with autocratic leadership. VB plans to invest $920,000 in its first physical flagship store in the Norwood shopping district, financed by $480,000 venture capital and $440,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 44,000 units a year. VB faces a growing operational problem: returns abuse has reached 13% of online orders, with buyers ordering multiple shades and sending almost all of them back.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement Extract — Q3 2026 Campaign: Velvette Beauty's social media campaign generated 2.4 million impressions, 58,000 clicks and a 2.9% conversion rate. 46 influencer posts averaged 310,000 views each. Average order value was $34.60, with 31,500 units sold online last quarter. The campaign cost $21,000, and 54% of buyers were aged 18-34. A retargeting email series achieved a 6.4% open-to-purchase rate, and 72% of new customers discovered VB through influencer content. The flagship store launch target is 900 first-month visitors a day.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Velvette Beauty as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.1% to 4.9%, raising borrowing costs across the economy. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.3% from $13.05 to $13.87 per hour from April 2026, increasing fulfilment and store-staff wage bills. (3) Botanical and packaging input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, cosmetics-price inflation is 6.6%, and consumer spending on online beauty grew 9.3% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VB intends to fund part of the flagship store launch with venture capital. Explain two advantages for VB of using venture capital instead of its $440,000 retained profit to fund the store.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Venture capital brings more than money: VB gains an investor with beauty and retail expertise, supplier contacts and board-level guidance on site selection in Norwood, lease negotiation and store design — knowledge a 38-person pure-player brand may lack as it opens its first physical shop. The money arrives without interest or repayment dates, protecting VB's cash while the $920,000 build is on site.

Point 2: Keeping the $440,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a working-capital buffer for the online operation that still drives 31,500 units a quarter, absorbing the 10.8% rise in botanical and packaging input costs and the 13% returns abuse before the store pays for itself. VB's backers also back the brand publicly, boosting credibility with landlords and landlords' lenders, and patient venture capital is more flexible than a bank if opening weekends underperform targets. It also strengthens the balance sheet with new equity, making VB more credible to the Norwood shopping district's letting agents and their lenders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Velvette Beauty, its store launch and its finances.

questions.question_text: VB is launching its first physical flagship store. Consider an influencer-led opening event, a national television campaign, or local radio sponsorship. Which should VB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Influencer-led opening event: VB's entire brand is built on influencer discovery — 46 posts averaged 310,000 views and 72% of new customers find VB through creators, with 54% of buyers aged 18-34. An in-store event with skincare demos, shade-matching and limited edition bundles would fill the 900 first-month visitor target, generate genuine user content from the venue itself, and convert online fans into walk-in buyers for the price of appearances and samples rather than airtime.

National television campaign: Television would deliver mass reach across the whole country and legitimise the brand as a mainstream beauty retailer, suiting VB's ambition beyond Norwood. But production and airtime are far beyond a brand spending $21,000 on a whole digital quarter, most of the audience cannot visit one Norwood store, and measuring sales response is weak — an unjustifiable spend for a launch of this scale.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio would speak directly to Norwood listeners with opening offers, parking directions and loyalty-card sign-ups, cheap and frequent. However, VB's core 18-34 audience streams rather than listens to radio, beauty is visual, and radio cannot demonstrate texture, shade and scent — the very attributes that close beauty sales in store.

Recommendation: VB should choose an influencer-led opening event. It speaks directly to the 18-34 creator-fuelled audience that already drives the webstore, costs a small fraction of television, is measurable through redemptions and online mentions, and showcases the omni-channel story — try in store, reorder online. Television is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful for a single flagship, and radio is rejected as unvisual and off-audience; VB can layer low-cost local PR and in-store sampling on top of the influencer anchor.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: VB operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for VB of autocratic leadership while launching its first physical store.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives Amara Osei a single, decisive chain of command at a moment when hundreds of launch decisions — store layout, pricing, opening hours, staff contracts and merchandising — must align quickly for a fixed $920,000 budget. Clear directives prevent paralysis, keep the fulfilment centre and store teams coordinated, and ensure brand standards are met from day one without lengthy consultation committees.

Point 2: A flat hierarchy means the 38 staff already answer directly to the founder, so the opening store inherits a culture of fast execution and no filtering of bad news. Autocratic direction is especially valuable in beauty retail, where opening week must deliver consistent service, shade matching and till accuracy instantly; problems flagged in the morning can be fixed by the afternoon, protecting the $34.60 average order value as the brand pivots from web-only to physical trading.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VB's launch, structure and leadership style.

questions.question_text: VB wants to cut picking errors and returns abuse running at 13% of orders. Consider a picking-accuracy bonus or profit sharing for its fulfilment staff. Which should VB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Picking-accuracy bonus: A measurable weekly bonus — for example, docked for mis-picked orders, wrong shades or wrong quantities — would directly attack the packing errors that drive the 13% returns rate, since VB can log every return against the picker and order. It is transparent, immediate, cheap to administer and highly visible to the fulfilment team; it concentrates minds on exactly the behaviour causing the problem. Its limits are that it narrowly rewards accuracy, not speed or customer care, and could make staff rush less — or game the metric by rejecting borderline orders, shifting work rather than eliminating mistakes.

Profit sharing: Sharing a percentage of quarterly online profit with all staff would lift morale across the whole business, reward everyone from packers to customer service, and motivate effort in areas tracking cannot capture — friendliness with customers, suggesting bundle alternatives, or flagging systemic stock issues. However, payouts reward total profit rather than the 13% returns defect specifically, are delayed and unpredictable (a bad quarter pays nothing), are small per head in a $16.00-unit model, and dilute VB's already-stretched $440,000 retained profit if margins are thin.

Decision: VB should choose a picking-accuracy bonus for fulfilment staff, reviewed quarterly, rather than across-the-board profit sharing. The returns problem is specific and measurable; a targeted bonus hits it directly, costs less than splitting profits, and fits the flat, autocratically led culture with clear targets and instant feedback. Profit sharing is rejected as the primary lever because it rewards diffuse outcomes, pays out for drivers VB cannot attribute to individuals, and weakens the urgent focus needed before the flagship store doubles order volume; VB can add a modest annual profit-sharing payout later, once the returns rate falls below 8%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to VB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of VB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of VB with a well-justified decision explaining why profit sharing is rejected as the primary lever and a picking-accuracy bonus is preferred.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: Break-even output = $270,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $7.00) = $270,000 ÷ $9.00 = 30,000 units; Margin of safety = 44,000 − 30,000 = 14,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 14,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $7.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. VB's managers can hold the 14,000-unit margin of safety against the flagship store's projected first-year sales to judge whether the launch rent, fit-out and staffing can be borne if online demand stays flat in the transition.
2. The $9.00 contribution per unit lets managers model bundle pricing, for example a skincare trio at $42 instead of $48, showing exactly how many units must move to keep each order above variable cost and cover store fixed overheads.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $270,000 and contribution, managers can test whether VB truly needs the $480,000 venture capital versus the $440,000 retained profit, and set online and store revenue checkpoints at which each funding slice is drawn down.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost ($270,000 ÷ 44,000 = $6.14, plus $7.00 = $13.14 per unit) and labour productivity (44,000 units ÷ 38 staff ≈ 1,158 units per worker) to spot warehouse inefficiency driving 13% returns abuse, and to brief the flagship store team on target throughput per shift.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 14,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 14,000-unit safety cushion vs 44,000-unit output and 30,000 break-even; bundle-pricing model vs $9.00 contribution; funding-drawdown feasibility for $480,000 venture capital vs $440,000 retained profit; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.14 with productivity of 1,158 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.58 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.93 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.02 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $285,000; 2025 current assets = $210,000 + $60,000 + $175,000 = $445,000. 2024 cover = $285,000 ÷ $180,000 current liabilities = 1.58; 2025 cover = $445,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.93. 2024 liquid cover = ($285,000 − $150,000) ÷ $180,000 = $135,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.75; 2025 liquid cover = ($445,000 − $210,000) ÷ $230,000 = $235,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.02.

Evaluation: VB's liquidity has strengthened substantially. Cash jumped from $90,000 to $175,000 as venture capital and retained profit were banked ahead of the store build, inventories rose only moderately from $150,000 to $210,000 (sensible for launch stock without over-ordering shades), and trade receivables, although small, rose from $45,000 to $60,000 as some influencer and wholesale partners pay on terms. Current liabilities climbed from $180,000 to $230,000, but current assets grew far faster. Non-current assets increased from $1,300,000 to $1,720,000 and capital employed from $1,405,000 to $1,725,000, consistent with fit-out spend on the flagship store. The strongest signal is that the liquid cover crossed 1.00 (1.02), meaning VB no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term obligations — valuable while the store is generating its first customers and before its cash position is proven.

Conclusion: VB's financial position has improved. Both cover measures rose, and the liquid measure moved above 1.00, giving VB genuine headroom into its first physical year. VB should still cap launch-stock depth to avoid shade obsolescence discounting, watch receivables from any retail partners, and preserve cash until the flagship hits its 900 first-month daily-visitor target and order volumes scale.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of cash, inventory and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether VB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VB of introducing refillable skincare packaging for its core moisturiser range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Refillable packaging would let VB charge a premium on its best-selling moisturiser while giving the 54% of buyers aged 18-34 — the most sustainability-conscious cohort in its campaign data — a visible reason to stay loyal. Refills lock customers into repeat purchasing, lowering customer-acquisition costs below the $21,000 quarterly campaign spend, differentiating VB on Norwood's shopping strip, and cutting packaging weight and cost per refill, partially offsetting the 10.8% rise in botanical input costs.

Disadvantage: Refill systems require new moulds, sealing line changeovers and consumer education on how to return or refill pods, upfront spending that competes with the $920,000 store budget. If refills are messy or hygiene perceptions fail, VB risks damaging the exact product whose shade and texture drive its $34.60 average order, and refill returns could worsen the 13% returns abuse if tracking does not identify whether empty pods came back with genuine refill intent or abusive free-merchandise claims.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VB's campaign data, costs and brand positioning.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.9%, the 6.3% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in botanical input costs will affect VB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (from 4.1% to 4.9%): VB carries no variable-rate bank debt — the $480,000 venture capital is equity and the $440,000 retained profit is free — so the direct interest impact is negligible. The rise instead makes later borrowing (for stock lines or store expansion) pricier and may cool consumers' willingness to use credit for premium beauty, though online beauty spending still grew 9.3%. This is the smallest of the three threats for VB, and it can be managed entirely by avoiding variable-rate borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (6.3% rise to $13.87 per hour from April 2026): VB's 38 staff span fulfilment packers, customer service and, from opening day, store advisors and till staff on hourly contracts. Only a minority of the team is salaried; the fulfilment and store floor is largely hourly. On an hourly wage base of roughly $260,000 a year, the 6.3% rise adds about $16,400 a year — noticeable but absorbable, especially if VB lifts shift productivity, multiskilling and the 900 first-month daily-visitor target converts to sales.

Input-cost inflation (10.8% rise in botanicals and packaging): botanical extracts and active ingredients dominate VB's $7.00 variable cost per unit — roughly $4.60 of it is spent on raw ingredients and jars. A 10.8% rise adds close to $0.50 per unit, or about $22,000 a year on 44,000 units, and squeezes the $9.00 contribution per unit toward $8.50. Worse, cosmetics-price inflation is 6.6%, so VB cannot fully pass the increase on without breaking its mid-market positioning against cheaper supermarket skincare.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in botanical input costs will have the greatest impact on VB. At roughly $22,000 a year it exceeds the $16,400 wage rise and the negligible interest effect, it is inseparable from product quality (the core of VB's reputation), and it compounds with every unit sold online and in-store. VB should respond by locking 12-month botanical supply contracts, introducing a small, phased price increase concentrated on hero products, launching a refill programme where consumers accept higher value per pump, and expanding margin-accretive accessories — while fixing store rosters efficiently so the wage increase stays a manageable second threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VB with a well-justified judgement that the input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
